q: Regarding infectious croup, which statement is TRUE?
o: It is a common indication for tracheostomy
Haemophilus influenzae type b is the usual cause
Corticosteroids are effective in relieving symptoms
e: Croup is viral (parainfluenza), and dexamethasone helps in all grades. The diagnosis is clinical.
k: corticosteroids are effective in all grades

q: All of the following are true of croup EXCEPT:
o: It is caused by a bacterial agent
Parainfluenza virus is the commonest cause
e: Croup is viral, so antibiotics are not part of the treatment.

q: Which step is NOT indicated in the management of croup?
o: Nebulised adrenaline for stridor at rest
e: Croup is viral; antibiotics are not useful.

q: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child has sudden high fever, drooling, a muffled voice and soft stridor. He sits leaning forward. What is the FIRST step?
o: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Insert an intravenous cannula and take blood cultures
Secure the airway by intubation in the operating theatre
e: This is epiglottitis: the child must not be upset. The airway is secured first, then intravenous ceftriaxone is given.

q: All of the following favour epiglottitis rather than viral croup EXCEPT:
o: Sudden onset without a preceding cold
e: A barking cough is typical of croup; epiglottitis has little or no cough.

q: A 6-week-old has had noisy breathing on inspiration since shortly after birth, worse with crying and with colds. He feeds and grows well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of chronic stridor in infants and resolves by 12–24 months.

q: A 2-year-old wakes at midnight with a barking cough and stridor but no fever; it settles quickly and has happened before. What is the diagnosis?
e: Spasmodic croup: sudden attacks at night without fever, recurrent, in an atopic child.

q: Which organism does NOT commonly cause acute otitis media?
e: Acute otitis media is caused by pneumococcus, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella and viruses; Pseudomonas is seen in chronic or neonatal infection.

q: An 8-year-old has fever, sore throat, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior neck nodes, no cough. What is the main aim of antibiotic treatment?
o: To shorten the illness by a week
To prevent otitis media with effusion
e: Penicillin given within 9 days of the start of the illness prevents rheumatic fever; it does not prevent glomerulonephritis.

q: A 15-year-old with exudative tonsillitis develops a widespread rash after amoxicillin; he has splenomegaly. What is the diagnosis?
e: Epstein–Barr virus infection causes exudative tonsillitis, enlarged nodes and splenomegaly, and amoxicillin causes a rash.

q: According to IMCI, a child with pus draining from the ear for 3 weeks should receive:
o: Ear wicking and topical quinolone drops
e: A chronic ear infection (pus for 14 days or more) is dried by wicking and treated with topical quinolone drops.

q: What is the commonest cause of conductive hearing loss in children?
e: Glue ear is the commonest cause, and it may delay speech.
k: commonest cause of conductive hearing loss

q: Which X-ray sign belongs to epiglottitis?
o: Steeple sign on the anteroposterior view
Thumb sign on the lateral neck view
e: Epiglottitis gives the thumb sign on the lateral view; croup gives the steeple sign on the anteroposterior view.
